It offers no way to remove an arbitrary (non-top) element and keeps no handle-to-position index, so cancellation is O(N); an indexed heap (handle -> heap index) is needed
mcqs.explanation: `std::priority_queue` exposes only push/top/pop — there is no arbitrary removal and no internal index, so cancelling a specific scheduled item means an O(N) scan. A scheduler that cancels frequently (in trading, most orders are cancelled before firing) needs an indexed binary heap that maintains a `handle -> current heap index` map, giving O(log N) cancel and reschedule (and keeping `pos_` in sync inside every swap).

mcqs.q: For a large population of short-lived, near-future timers (order TTLs, retransmits, rate-limit refills), which structure beats a min-heap, and how?
options: A timing wheel — a circular array of buckets with intrusive lists — giving O(1) insert, O(1) cancel, and O(1)-amortized expiry, versus the heap's O(log N) per operation
A balanced BST, giving O(1) insert
A hash map keyed by deadline, giving O(1) next-deadline lookup
A sorted std::vector, giving O(1) everything
mcqs.explanation: A timing wheel hashes a timer due in `d` ticks into bucket `(current + d) % WHEEL_SIZE` and advances a hand each tick; insert and intrusive-unlink cancel are O(1), and firing a bucket is O(1) amortized. Far-future timers are handled with a per-node `rounds` counter (hashed wheel) or hierarchical wheels. The heap's strength is a cheap O(1) next-deadline peek and natural far-future support, which is why it suits a simulation/backtest event loop; the wheel wins for many near-future timers. Use power-of-two `WHEEL_SIZE` for bitwise wrap and intrusive allocation-free nodes.

mcqs.q: Matching an incoming aggressive order against the book walks resting levels from the best price. What is its complexity, and what keeps best-bid/ask maintenance cheap as levels empty?
options: O(log L) per fill because levels live in a balanced tree

O(fills + levels-walked): it fills FIFO from the head of each level and advances to the next occupied level; best is tracked incrementally and reseated by a short, cache-resident scan (or a bitset + TZCNT for O(1))
O(L) every match because the whole ladder must be rescanned
O(1) regardless of how many orders are filled
mcqs.explanation: Matching is output-sensitive: it fills from the FIFO head of the best level, unlinks filled orders, and when a level empties walks to the next occupied level, so the cost is O(number of fills + number of levels crossed). Best bid/ask are maintained incrementally rather than recomputed; when the touched level empties, reseating the best is an amortized-O(1) short scan because the next occupied level is usually a tick or two away and cache-resident, and a bitset of occupied levels with TZCNT/std::countr_zero makes it O(1) worst-case.

coding.prompt: Implement the core of a single-symbol limit order book over a dense integer-tick price range, with zero hot-path allocation. Each price level is an intrusive FIFO of orders; `add` and `cancel(order_id)` are O(1); best bid/ask are tracked incrementally (reseat to the next occupied level when one empties). Constructor: `OrderBook(Price lo, Price hi, std::size_t maxOrders)`. Operations: `add(OrderId, Side, Price, Qty)` and `cancel(OrderId)`. Read-only accessors (`best_bid`, `best_ask`, `level_qty`, `has_order`, `front_id`) are provided for the tests.
hints: Orders carry intrusive prev/next links and live in a preallocated pool; allocate via a free list.
A direct-addressed `vector<Level>` indexed by (price - base) gives O(1) level access; a Level holds head/tail and an aggregate qty.
An unordered_map<OrderId, Order*> makes cancel O(1): look up, intrusive unlink, return node to the pool.
coding.discussion: The design buys O(1) add/cancel/modify and amortized-O(1) best tracking with zero hot-path allocation. Orders live in a preallocated pool with a free list, so `add` and `cancel` never call the allocator. The direct-addressed `levels_` array makes locating a price level a single index computation (no tree, no hashing). Each level is an intrusive doubly-linked FIFO, so `cancel` unlinks an arbitrary order in O(1) once `by_id_` locates it. Best bid/ask are maintained incrementally with a cheap compare on add; when a level empties at the touch, `reseat_best` walks to the next occupied level — amortized O(1) because the next level is usually a tick or two away and stays cache-resident (a bitset of occupied levels plus `TZCNT`/`countr_zero` gives O(1) worst-case). Trade-offs: memory is proportional to the price range and it requires dense integer ticks; sparse prices need a hash-of-levels plus a sorted next-best structure. Variants: market-by-price drops the per-order lists and `by_id_` (just level aggregates); top-of-book is four numbers; many symbols is an array of books indexed by symbol id. Single-writer, no locks on the matching thread; price-up/size-up modify is cancel+add (loses time priority), size-down is in place (keeps it).

coding.prompt: Implement an indexed min-heap timer scheduler supporting `schedule(when, action) -> Handle` (O(log N)), `cancel(Handle)` (O(log N)), and `poll(now, sink)` firing all due items. The index must support O(log N) cancel of an arbitrary scheduled item.
hints: Store nodes in a contiguous vector; keep an unordered_map<Handle, size_t> from handle to current heap index.
Every swap during sift-up/sift-down must update the position map for both moved handles.
Cancel = locate via the map, swap with the last element, pop, then sift the moved element.
coding.discussion: A binary min-heap keyed by `when` gives O(log N) schedule and O(1) peek of the next deadline. The piece `std::priority_queue` cannot provide is arbitrary cancel: here a `pos_` map tracks each handle's current heap index, and crucially every `swap_nodes` updates `pos_` for both moved handles, so cancel locates its element in O(1) and removes it in O(log N) (swap with last, pop, then re-sift). `poll` fires everything due and hands the action to a sink, letting the caller choose to run inline or enqueue onto a worker. This heap is the right choice for a simulation/backtest event loop with arbitrary (possibly far-future) deadlines. For a large population of short-lived near-future timers (order TTLs, retransmits) a timing wheel is better: O(1) insert/cancel/expiry via intrusive bucket lists, with a `rounds` counter or hierarchical wheels for longer ranges. Low-latency notes: pre-reserve the heap, avoid `std::function` in the very hottest loop (use an enum+payload or function pointer + context), read the clock once per `poll` rather than per timer, and keep the scheduler single-writer with producers feeding via an SPSC ring.

mcqs.q: What mechanism underlies a type trait like `is_pointer<T>`, and what is its runtime cost?
options: A `dynamic_cast` chain; cost grows with inheritance depth
A lookup in a global type registry at startup
Partial template specialization (compile-time pattern matching); inheriting from `std::true_type`/`std::false_type` gives a free `::value` — zero runtime cost
A runtime `typeid` comparison; cost is one virtual call
mcqs.explanation: Traits are metafunctions implemented via partial specialization: a primary template (e.g. `: std::false_type`) plus a specialization that matches the pattern (e.g. `template<class T> struct is_pointer<T*> : std::true_type`). The compiler picks the matching specialization and the answer is a compile-time constant `::value`; nothing about it exists at runtime. This is what powers tag dispatch and `if constexpr` branch selection at zero cost.

mcqs.q: Which technique detects, at compile time, whether a type `T` has a nested `::value_type`?
options: A runtime reflection call
`dynamic_cast<typename T::value_type*>`
Overloading `operator.` for `T`
SFINAE with `std::void_t`: a primary `false_type` template plus a partial specialization keyed on `std::void_t<typename T::value_type>`
mcqs.explanation: The detection idiom uses `std::void_t`: `template<class T, class = void> struct has_value_type : std::false_type {};` and `template<class T> struct has_value_type<T, std::void_t<typename T::value_type>> : std::true_type {};`. If `typename T::value_type` is a valid type, the specialization is viable (SFINAE keeps it in the overload set) and resolves to `true_type`; otherwise it is silently discarded and the primary `false_type` is chosen. C++20 concepts (`requires`) express the same intent more readably.

mcqs.q: In a generic `copy(T* dst, const T* src, size_t n)`, you want a `memcpy` fast path for trivially-copyable types and an element-wise loop otherwise, with no runtime branch. Which is the cleanest correct approach?
options: `if constexpr (std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>)` choose memcpy, else the loop — the untaken branch is discarded at compile time (tag dispatch on `std::is_trivially_copyable<T>{}` is the C++14 equivalent)
`reinterpret_cast` plus `memcpy` unconditionally
A runtime `if (is_trivially_copyable)` check
A `virtual` method on `T`
mcqs.explanation: `if constexpr` (C++17) evaluates the condition at compile time and discards the untaken branch — so the `memcpy` path is emitted for trivially-copyable `T` and the element-wise loop for others, with no runtime branch to predict and the dead branch not even required to compile for the current type. The pre-C++17 equivalent is tag dispatch: overload on `std::true_type`/`std::false_type` and call with `std::is_trivially_copyable<T>{}`. Both are zero runtime cost.

mcqs.q: Does marking a function `constexpr` guarantee it runs at compile time?
options: Yes, but only at `-O2` or higher

No — `constexpr` is permission: it runs at compile time only in a constant-expression context (or if assigned to a `constexpr` result); with runtime arguments it runs at runtime. `consteval` forces compile-time
No — `constexpr` always runs at runtime; only macros run at compile time
Yes — every `constexpr` call is evaluated by the compiler
mcqs.explanation: `constexpr` on a function means it *may* be evaluated at compile time, not that it must be. Called in a constant-expression context (e.g. `constexpr auto x = f(10);`, an array bound, a `static_assert`) it is folded by the compiler; called with runtime arguments the very same function executes at runtime. If you require compile-time evaluation, either bind the result to a `constexpr`/`static_assert`, or declare the function `consteval` (an immediate function), which is an error if it cannot be evaluated at compile time.

mcqs.q: What does `constinit` (C++20) guarantee, and how does it differ from `const`?
options: It is a synonym for `constexpr`
It forces the object onto the stack
It guarantees constant (static) initialization — no dynamic init, fixing the static-init-order fiasco — but the object remains mutable; `const` is about immutability, not init time
It makes the object immutable like `const` but also compile-time
mcqs.explanation: `constinit` requires that a static/thread-local variable be initialized with a constant initializer (no runtime dynamic initialization), which avoids the static-initialization-order fiasco — but the variable is still mutable afterward (`++g_counter` is fine). `const` concerns immutability and says nothing about *when* initialization happens. `constexpr` implies both constant init and `const`. The three are may/must/init-time-but-mutable distinctions: `constexpr` (may run at compile time, const), `consteval` (must), `constinit` (constant init, mutable).

mcqs.q: How does CRTP (`struct Circle : Shape<Circle>`) achieve polymorphic-style dispatch with zero runtime overhead?
options: It uses a hidden vtable that is faster than the normal one
It performs a `dynamic_cast` that the compiler optimizes away
It stores a function pointer per object that the compiler inlines
The base is templated on the derived type, so it can `static_cast<Derived&>(*this)` and call the derived method directly; the call is resolved and inlined at compile time, with no vptr
mcqs.explanation: Because `Shape<Circle>` is instantiated knowing the concrete derived type, the base can `static_cast` `*this` to `Derived&` (the `.self()` cast) and call the derived implementation directly. The compiler resolves the target at compile time and inlines it — no vptr, no indirect call, and the optimizer can fold across the (now eliminated) call boundary. The cost is that `Shape<Circle>` and `Shape<Square>` are unrelated types, so you cannot keep them in one heterogeneous container.

mcqs.q: What is the key limitation of CRTP compared to runtime (`virtual`) polymorphism?
options: You cannot store different CRTP instantiations in one heterogeneous container, because `Base<A>` and `Base<B>` share no common base type
CRTP cannot inline the dispatched call
CRTP suffers from object slicing that virtual does not
CRTP objects always carry an 8-byte vptr
mcqs.explanation: CRTP trades runtime type erasure for zero-overhead static dispatch. Since `Base<A>` and `Base<B>` are distinct, unrelated types, there is no common base pointer to collect them under, so a `std::vector<Base*>` of mixed shapes is impossible. When you need a heterogeneous (but closed) set, use `std::variant` + `std::visit`, or erase to a type-erasing facade only at the boundary while keeping CRTP inside the hot loop. (Slicing is a value-semantics hazard of runtime polymorphism; it does not arise with CRTP.)

mcqs.q: Which standard-library facility is itself an example of CRTP?
options: `std::function`
`std::enable_shared_from_this<T>` (you write `class T : public std::enable_shared_from_this<T>`)
`std::variant`
`std::shared_ptr`'s control block
mcqs.explanation: `std::enable_shared_from_this<T>` is the canonical standard-library CRTP: you derive `class Widget : public std::enable_shared_from_this<Widget>`, so the base is parameterized on the derived type and can hand back a correct `shared_ptr<Widget>` to `this`. It is the textbook "where have you seen CRTP in the stdlib?" answer. (Boost.Operators-style comparison mixins are another classic use, now largely replaced by the C++20 spaceship `<=>`.)
